utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Bouckaert, could I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And, Mr. Bouckaert, let me remind both you and me of the need to speak a bit slowly and pause between question and answer, to assist the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can return for a moment to what was marked for identification as Exhibit -- as P352. Mr. Bouckaert, this is at tab 36 of your binder. It is the report that you drafted entitled "Crimes Against Civilians." And if we could turn to what is page 17 of the English version, and the bottom of page 18 in the Macedonian version. The English version that I'm talking about has ERN number U0000114. I'm wondering -- I don't know if there's a problem with the -- ah, here it's changing now. There we are. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, we need your assistance to clarify a couple of things, please. Do you see in the middle of page 17 in the English version there is a subtitle called "The Role of the International Community"; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And below that, we see in bold letters: "Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The penultimate sentence of the next paragraph says this: "Although the mandate," and we're talking about the mandate of the OSCE, "does not explicitly reference human rights, activities in the OSCE's 'human dimension' are certainly implicit in the mandate and have formed part of the missions' work for years." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next paragraph tells us this: "At least two OSCE international observers were present in Ljuboten on Tuesday, August 14th, 2001, when international observers and journalists first gained access to the village after the government offensive. According to the international journalists who were on the scene, the OSCE monitors carefully documented the physical evidence at the scene with a video camera, and they spoke to villagers about the events in Ljuboten." Do you see what I've just read to you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, moving on to, in the same paragraph, onto the next page, which is page 18 in the English version, it says: "The OSCE mission has issued no public report of this investigation." And now we're at -- it's page 19 now in the Macedonian version: "One of the OSCE monitors, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed to the Associated Press that the OSCE had found the remains of five persons in the village, including an elderly man, and suggested that they might have been killed while running away." The next paragraph, you describe -- you, as the author of the report, describe how the Minister of the Interior, Ljube Boskoski, immediately and fiercely criticised the OSCE for even attempting to investigate the events in Ljuboten. And then we see a quote from Mr. Boskoski from the 14th of August. And then in the next paragraph that begins: "During a meeting ...," it says that: "The then OSCE head of mission, Ambassador Carlo Ungaro reportedly distanced himself from the reported comments of his OSCE monitors." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the next full paragraph, it begins: "The OSCE's continuing silence ..." Do you see that phrase?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says: "The OSCE's continuing silence about the serious abuses committed by police in Ljuboten is disturbing because the organisation undoubtedly has sufficient information to speak out publicly about the events in Ljuboten and demand a credible and impartial investigation." Then you go on to say that: "The OSCE silence has helped the Macedonian government maintain its version of the events in Ljuboten and avoid further investigation." The next paragraph, which is at the bottom of page 18 in the English version, is on page 20 of the Macedonian version, and there is a critical -- a sentence, the first sentence of that paragraph, that that says: "The OSCE mission in Skopje has remained largely silent on the grave human rights abuses that have been committed by the Macedonian forces throughout the conflict." Do you see what I've just read to you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We turn to the next page in the English version, please, which is page 19. We're still on page 20 of the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour. Perhaps as a matter of clarification, for the sake of cross-examination later on, we would like to know from the Prosecution what's the purpose of this exercise of reading the statement attributed to Mr. Bouckaert in relation to the OSCE. None of those statements were put to Mr. Bolton when he was present in this courtroom, and we're just wondering whether the Prosecution is now minded to attack the OSCE with OSCE for its conduct in Macedonia in general in relation to Ljuboten in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon. I want to explore with the witness who wrote this report why he wrote this section of the report and why he wrote this criticism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying you're doing that with an open mind or you have a purpose? What reliance are you going to make upon this in due course?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That -- well, obviously that will depend on the witness's answer, but the -- depending on the witness's answer, the effect may have a certain impact on the Chamber's reliance on at least some of the OSCE documents that have been used to date in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, I would simply insist on upon the fact that none of those documents were either challenged or taken on with Mr. Bolton, who was the best person to deal with those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're in a rather awkward position, Mr. Saxon. It's your own evidence, and now, by this approach, you're seeking to take away from its quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's not -- I don't believe that's quite -- I don't believe that's quite correct, Your Honour. I'm not attacking through this evidence the evidence of Mr. Bolton, if that is the concern of Your Honour. I'm -- I have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, it's the fact that you are wanting to deal with matters that you could and should have with Mr. Bolton but did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, to what is tab 38 in your binder, Mr. Bouckaert, and this is 65 ter number 333. It has -- begins with ERN number N002-5867. Do you recognise this, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the press release that was released when we released the report "Crimes Against Civilians."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you say "we," who released this report?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drafted the press release and Human Rights Watch, as an organisation, released the press release and the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you tell us to whom this press release would have been sent to?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As is our standard practice, it goes to our media, diplomat, and authority list, which includes thousands of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, if this report, dated September 5th, 2001, could be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P353, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can turn now, please, to what is -- actually, before I ask you to turn, I need to ask you, Mr. Bouckaert: Prior to the publication of the report that you wrote about the events in Ljuboten, did another -- did a media source receive some information about the expected contents of your report?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, to what should be tab 39 in your binder. This is 65 ter number 334. It begins with ERN N002-5869.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is an article from "The Sunday Telegraph." It's dated the 26th of August, 2001. There is a headline: "Massacre Report Names Macedonia Interior Minister." Then below at the start of the article it says: "Macedonia's hard-line Interior Minister will come under pressure this week to explain his role in the worst alleged atrocity in the 6-month conflict with ethnic Albanian rebels." And then below that it says: "Ljube Boskoski will be accused by Human Rights Watch, an American-based pressure group, of involvement in the incident in Ljuboten." Below that, we see: "The accusation will be made in a damning report to be submitted to the Macedonian government." And then, lower down, it mentions you, Peter Bouckaert, senior researcher with Human Rights Watch, who was writing the report, after a series of interviews with witnesses, said: "However, that the document would detail a massacre and raise questions about Mr. Boskoski's role." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although I don't think I used the word "massacre" when I spoke to the journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Is the remainder of the information correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall whether Mr. Boskoski responded to the information contained in this "Sunday Telegraph" article after it was published on the 26th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may just explain, this article was a result of a misunderstanding with a journalist. We didn't want any information about our investigation being released while I was still in country and before the report was released, so we were not very happy that she published this story. It was featured on the Evening News in Macedonia in Macedonian. I watched that newscast at my apartment. Obviously, I couldn't understand everything that was being said, but there was a discussion of the article, events in the "Sunday Telegraph" and Human Rights Watch and Peter Bouckaert, and then -- which I think was the journalist just reading this article in Macedonian. And then it featured Minister Boskoski responding to the allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. And what reactions or comments did you receive after Mr. Boskoski appeared on television commenting on this newspaper article?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soon thereafter I was contacted by two prominent ethnic Macedonians, including somebody who was within the government, who advised me to leave the country as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point I was busy with an investigation -- I had completed my Ljuboten investigation, and I was busy investigating the disappearances of ethnic Macedonians at the hand of the NLA, the Albanian rebel group, especially in the Tetovo area, and most of those ethnic Macedonians and ethnic Albanians who had disappeared at the hands of the NLA were former police officers. So that work required extensive contacts with the police to contact the families of these disappeared people. I contacted my executive director, Elizabeth Anderson, in New York by cellphone. We discussed this unanticipated newspaper article and the reaction of Mr. Boskoski, as well as the unfeasibility of continuing with the research on the disappearances at the hands of the NLA. So I took a flight out the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender the document at tab 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P354, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Actually, I apologise. I should have said "Tab 39" "39," my mistake. I was thinking ahead. If we could move, please, to what is tab 41 in your binder, Mr. Bouckaert. This is 65 ter number 335. It has ERN number N002-5871. This is an article from the BBC, dated the 27th of August, 2001. It's entitled "Macedonia's Interior Minister Rejects Human Rights Accusations," and it begins: "Macedonia Interior Minister Ljube Boskoski has strongly denied claims that he was involved in an alleged atrocity against ethnic Albanians two weeks ago, Macedonian Radio said on Monday." And then the radio said that Mr. Boskoski was responding to "The Sunday Telegraph" report. And down below, and it says: "Asked by the radio to comment," Mr. Boskoski is quoted as saying: "I vigorously reject the accusations against the Interior Ministry and against the regular and reserve police forces, which have demonstrated unprecedented courage in defending Macedonia's sovereignty." The next paragraph: "I view the accusations issued by the Human Rights Watch as a classic act of framing the Interior Minister." Mr. Bouckaert, were you provided with all newspaper articles that were related to the work that you were doing in 2001?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how were you provided with this information?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have support staff in New York who monitor the media on a daily basis, to send me all information about the countries I'm working on which they think is relevant, and this is actually an article which was provided by me to the Tribunal from my files. I should mention that it's not a BBC article, it's a translation of a story on Macedonian Radio on August 27th, as is indicated by the source information at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I appreciate that. At the top, we see: "BBC Monitoring News File"?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this item, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply to register the objection which we have made at the time in relation to the reliability of this piece, and the fact that Mr. Bouckaert has not given any evidence about the accuracy or truthfulness of the content of that document. We'll say no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be received as Exhibit P355, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn now to what is tab 40. This is 65 ter number 335. I apologise. 65 ter number 992. It starts with ERN number N002-5903.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, that's tab 41 in my binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. It's tab 40 in my binder. Well, then let's call it tab 41. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the article on the screen is actually not in my --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Actually, if we turn to page 7 of this ERN range, we'll find the article that I'm looking for. There we see it. This is an article published on "The New York Times" front page September 5th, 2001, entitled "Report Says Macedonians Killed Civilians in Revenge." It's by a journalist named Ian Fisher. And this article contains information about what I see in the third full paragraph: "In a detailed report to be issued today, Human Rights Watch accuses overwhelmingly Slavic forces of Macedonia's government of summary execution of civilians, arson and torture." In the right-hand column, there's a reference to Mr. Boskoski. Do you see that, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Mr. Boskoski is quoted as responding to some of the accusations in the Human Rights Watch report. Can we turn to the next page, please. On the next page, it's a little bit difficult to see on the screen, but in the first full paragraph it begins with the words: "Mr. Bouckaert ..." Actually, even in the very first paragraph, there's a reference to Peter Bouckaert, a senior researcher for Human Rights Watch, who wrote the group's report on Ljuboten. So were you interviewed by the journalist who prepared this article?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender this article, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I would simply make the same point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P356, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn to what I hope is tab 42 in your binder, Mr. Bouckaert. It is 65 ter number 337. It has ERN number N002-5874.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, this is an article from the Associated Press, dated the 5th of September, 2001. Again, it's a discussion of the Human Rights Watch report that you authoured, and there's a discussion -- there's a sentence in the middle describing how the report also implicated Interior Minister Ljube Boskoski in the bloodshed. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Down below, two paragraphs further on, we see the words: "But Boskoski vehemently rejected the allegations, saying he arrived only after the end of the operation." The next paragraph, Mr. Boskoski is quoted as saying he would seek legal recourse at the European Court of Human Rights to clear his name. And in the next paragraph, Mr. Boskoski is quoted as saying: "I want to end this speculation and these lies presented by this quasi-international organisation,' Boskoski said." Do you see that, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please. The next page, sort of in the middle of the page, there's a sentence beginning: "Macedonian police unions ..." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says: "Macedonian police unions issued a statement accusing Human Rights Watch of 'Remaining deaf and mute to claims of attacks against Macedonian authorities and civilians and threats of liquidation of entire families'." Then below that: "This organisation persistently sees violation of human rights on one side and one side alone, that of the allegedly-wronged Albanian minority." Mr. Bouckaert, do you feel that that is a fair and correct statement?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I thought it was one of the most unfair and personally hurtful statements that were issued against my organisation during the work, considering the work that we had done. The demonstrable dedication we had shown to monitoring violations by all sides to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. We will get to this. This particular article, would this have been sent to you by your colleagues in 2001?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, we will make the same point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I also saw the original statement from the Macedonian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P357, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps, Your Honour, instead of disturbing the next time, I would simply indicate that the point should be made in addition to the other articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn to what is hopefully tab 43 in your binder, Mr. Bouckaert. This is 65 ter number 336. It has ERN number N002-5872. It's an article from "The Times" dated the 6th of September, 2001, headlining or titled "Skopje Minister in Revenge-Raid Village." It begins by talking about how the Macedonian forces under the control of the country's Interior Minister launched a revenge raid against an ethnic Albanian village "last month." Do you see that, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then it says: "The New York-based Human Rights Watch highlighted the presence of Ljube Boskoski, the Interior Minister, in the village of Ljuboten on the third day of the raid when some of the Albanian civilians were killed." In the sixth paragraph, we see that after the raid on Ljuboten, there's a reference to Mr. Boskoski insisting that the village was a bastion of ethnic Albanian rebels and claimed that the only casualties were terrorists. Can we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may just point out, Mr. Boskoski contradicted himself in "The New York Times" story where he said he didn't know whether the people killed were rebels or civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we turn to the second page of this article, the top paragraph says: "During a Sunday house-to-house attack, police forces shot dead six civilians. One man was killed by police as he tried to close the door to his home," et cetera. Did this information -- did that come from the report that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as the prior paragraph indicates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this article, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P358, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn to what is hopefully tab 44 in your binder, Mr. Bouckaert. This is 65 ter number 338. It has ERN N002-5876 at the top. It comes from the BBC monitoring European. It's dated the 6th of September, 2001, and there's a title: "Minister Threatens Law Suit Over Claim of Human Rights Violations." And below we see the text of a report in English by the Macedonian state news agency, and below: "Skopje, 6 September," and there's a quote from the Macedonian Minister of the Interior, Ljube Boskoski: "I will press charges to the Court for human rights in Strasbourg because the claims of the Human Rights Watch organisation undermine not only the dignity of the Macedonian Ministry of Interior but also my personal dignity." Do you see that, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you have received this article in 2001?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of these -- a lot of the quotes in the previous article came from the press conference that Mr. Boskoski gave, which is referred to in the next paragraph of this statement. That's why the quotes are all so similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P359, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can turn, please, to what should be tab 45 in your binder, Mr. Bouckaert. This is 65 ter number 339. This is an article from "The New York Times" by a man named Ian Fisher. It's dated the 12th of August, 2001, and it says -- it's titled "Macedonians Kidnapped by Guerrillas Tell of Abuse," and the start of the article says: "A human rights group released detailed interviews today it conducted with roadworkers kidnapped by Albanian guerrillas this week in which the workers say they were tortured, forced to perform sexual acts on each other, and had initials carved into their backs." Below that paragraph, we see a victim saying he asked everyone for their names," one of the kidnapped men told a researcher with Human Rights Watch. Mr. Bouckaert, who was the researcher with Human Rights Watch referred to in this article?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be me, as is reflected at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how did the author of this article receive the information contained in this article?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I read my interview notes to him and to another journalist with "The Guardian."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, how you came to investigate the torture and other crimes committed against this group of roadworkers?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was contacted by somebody in the Macedonian Ministry of Information, who informed me that these five men had been released, that they were in the hospital in Kumanovo, and asked me if I would be interested in interviewing them. I was the only person contacted by the Ministry of Information. He then put me in contact with police officials in Kumanovo, who facilitated the interview for me, who actually took me to the hospital to interview one of the victims in the hospital and later took me to the house of a second person, who had been released from the hospital, to interview that second person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just for the record, who, then, did you conclude was responsible for these crimes?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people responsible for these crimes were members of the NLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And in October of that year, as the conflict came to an end, we actually wrote a letter to the then late president and the Prime Minister, asking that these serious crimes be excluded from the amnesty which was under consideration for the NLA because of their seriousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And again when you say "we," you're referring to Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P360, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn, Mr. Bouckaert, to what is hopefully tab 46 in your binder. It has 65 ter number 345. This is a document entitled "Police Abuse Against Albanians Continues in Macedonia, Peace Agreement Doesn't End Violence." It's dated the 22nd of August, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a press release I wrote about yet another case of police abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During what time period?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened on August 13th in the capital, Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P361, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn very briefly to what was admitted yesterday as Exhibit P334, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, you will recall this is the sketch that you drew based on the sketches that you drew when you were in Ljuboten on the 23rd of August. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm wondering if we can see this perhaps as a single image.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you mentioned yesterday, when we were looking at this sketch, that you recorded the burning of a home owned by an ethnic Macedonian by the name of Zlatko. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that home is just to the right and above the words "Ulica 5"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says "Macedonian house of Zlatko burned Thursday."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Just below the road and to the left at that point, there is another home which has the words under it: "Burned on Friday," and I'm wondering if the Court Usher could assist us by placing the magnifying glass over that square, so we can read the name of the person who owned that home. No, move to the right, please. No, nope. I'm sorry, can you please go back to where the magnifying glass was? All right, now just move a bit to the right, a bit more, now a little bit down. Can we have that -- Are you able to read the name, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will attempt to. It seems like it says "Rashad Kamberi."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that would have been the home of an ethnic Albanian that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Which was burned on the Friday after the 12th of August?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, at this time I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon, Mr. Bouckaert. My name is Guenal Mettraux, and together with Ms. Residovic, I'm appearing on behalf of Mr. Boskoski. Your Honour, perhaps before I start, there is a document that I will show early on to the witness, and my colleague Mr. Saxon and myself were being asked questions by the Chamber in relation to that particular document. We would simply like to indicate, and I believe the Prosecution agrees with it, that in a recent filing which relates to a Prosecution application to tender a number of documents relating to the destruction of houses, the Defence made reference to a particular OSCE document which we failed to attach. In turn, Mr. Saxon referred to the same document in his reply. We would simply indicate that the document to which both parties were referring was a document which has now been admitted into evidence as Exhibit 1D32, and I will show the document to this witness early on in the cross-examination, so simply to answer the question of the Chamber, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, I understand in your statement you indicated that you arrived in Macedonia during your fourth visit on the 17th of August of 2001. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct also that at the time of your arrival, there was no other investigator or researcher of Human Rights Watch on the ground in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that also correct that after the incident in Ljuboten, you were the first representative of Human Rights Watch to visit Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that also correct that between the period of time of 18th of August until the 25th of August, you carried out approximately 22 interviews with a number of -- with villagers?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure where that number came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Counsel has simply counted the number of references to different witnesses in your statement. Does that mean that you've referred to each and every interview?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can you recall how many interviews you've rejected or not --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would not have been rejected. They would've just not been included because they would have been repetitive of information already included.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can you recall approximately how many of those were not included in the report?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that the total number of interviews is probably between 35 and 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And would I be correct to understand that a 1-week investigation is a short or very short investigation by "Human Rights Watch" standards?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've carried out similar short investigations into similar or less serious incidents such as the IDF attack on the refugee attack in Jenin in the West Bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct or that in Jenin case you said that mission would last for a period of two weeks, anywhere up two or three months; would that be for such an investigation?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was a particularly long mission and it was focusing on a wide variety of incidents. The purpose of my visit in August was specifically to investigate Ljuboten, first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And could you tell this Chamber where these interviews took place, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The majority of the interviews took place in private homes in Skopje. We went and tracked down people who had been displaced from Ljuboten during the fighting or who had been released from custody and then interviewed them in private.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did some of the meetings also take place at the office of the DPA political party in Skopje?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. We had contact with the DPA, but I don't think any witnesses were interviewed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So if someone were to give that evidence, that would be incorrect, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just don't recall holding any interviews at the DPA office in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you tell who organised those meetings for you, who made the arrangements for you to meet and identify and locate these villagers?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you get any assistance from anyone from the village?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we started identifying villagers, we would ask them for the location of people who had been released from Ljuboten or for specific persons such as relatives and eyewitnesses to particular incidents, and then those villagers that we had found would put us in touch with other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that correct that during the 20 or so days, between the 17th of August when you arrived in the country and the 5th of September, when you published the report, you also carried out an on-site investigation, I understand, on the 23rd of August of 2001?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Would that be correct to suggest that you had announced the visit to the persons which you had interviewed in the days prior to that date?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so, no. You mean to all of the people we interviewed?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No, to some of the people, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we asked for contact information for the people in the village, but I don't think a large number of people knew about our visit to Ljuboten, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But some of them did?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct that your intention, at the time when deciding to visit Ljuboten, was to collect evidence of any violations of any humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And as I understand it, this is one of the objectives of your organisation, to bring those whom you consider to be responsible for such violations to justice. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although we don't remove any evidence. We look at the evidence that we see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No one would accuse you of that, Mr. Bouckaert. Is that also correct that one of the goals of your organisation is, to the extent possible, to assist the Office of the Prosecution in tracking down or at least in assisting the Prosecution in its investigation of violations of humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have always been fully cooperative with the Yugoslav Tribunal, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that was the case in relation to Ljuboten; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- after the report was published, we immediately sent a copy to the Tribunal, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts during that period prior to sending this report to the Office of the Prosecution with any member of the Office of the Prosecution? And I'm speaking of the period between the 17th and the 5th of September. Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not. I believe I was contacted by a member of the OTP on September 6th or September 7th to -- they expressed interest in the events in Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to perhaps start where you ended up yesterday in relation to questions which were asked of you about your observation about the destruction of houses. I think you will recall making a number of mentions about accelerators that it was your understanding, or in any case your belief, that accelerators had been used to burn houses. Can you recall this?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you have any evidence -- did you make any -- take any substance which you understood to be accelerant or was it simply based on your experience, as you explained, of observation in other conflicts?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was based on my own observations and during our visit to the village of Ljuboten, which were consistent with accounts of eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you didn't make any -- you didn't take any samples or any sort, you didn't find any traces of accelerants yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to be shown P339 at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, this is a picture that you were shown yesterday by the Prosecution. It's one of the pictures that you were shown yesterday. And you made an observation, when asked by my colleague, as to the nature or the cause, rather, of the destruction of particular houses, and you've indicated that it was your understanding that the presence of chimneys on a number of houses was an indication that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt. Just I was wondering could we wait until the photograph appears on the screen before the question? Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Absolutely. I apologise to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton [sic], you've made a number of comments --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert. Mr. Bouckaert, you've made a number of comments pursuant to questions of Mr. Saxon relating to the presence or the fact that chimneys were standing up on a number of houses which had incurred damage, and you explained to the Prosecution that you understood this to be an indication that the house had been burned rather than shelled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was not talking about the fact that a particular chimney was standing but that the chimneys of all the homes that we inspected were still standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct also, Mr. Bouckaert, that the chimneys in the village, in particular of those houses which you observed, were all attached to the wall and not to the roof of those houses, such as the one in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that's correct. I think that there were some chimneys which were more in the center of the home. This is the chimney of a store.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But would you agree that a number of houses which you observed yesterday in the picture, the chimney was attached to the wall rather than to the roof?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Are you able, sir, to estimate approximately how many houses make up the village of Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information, the -- Ljuboten has a population of 3.000 people. So based on that, I would guess there are probably about 400 to 600 homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And did you inquire with the villagers why particular areas or pockets of Ljuboten were targeted but not others; is that a matter that you raised with them?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: For the benefit of the interpreters, could the speakers please pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, would you like me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I see the question on the screen. We did ask and they had no particular answer for us on why this area of the village was so heavily damaged or had been the focus of the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness now please be shown what is Rule 65 ter 1D432, and it has an ERN range of 1D003979 to 3980, and the Macedonian version is a 1-page document -- no, 2-page document, 1D003977 to 3978.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I would just like to go through the top of that document first with you, Mr. Bouckaert. As you can see, it's a document that comes from Security and Counter-Intelligence Division, also known as the UBK of the Ministry of Interior, and it's the department of Cair. It has a number and it's dated the 19th of March of 2002. If I may draw your attention to the title of that document, it says: "The meetings took place on 12th and 14th of March of 2002," and then it locates the place where the meeting took place, and further down on this document there is a subject heading and it says: "Information and intelligence of interest to you UBK." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: At this stage, Mr. Bouckaert, I would like to show you the second page of this document. If the Registry could turn to the second page. I understand it's the second page in Macedonian as well. I should have pointed out to you that the person to whom the UBK spoke was given the nickname of Odja, and if I may draw your attention to the paragraph which starts: "At the end of the meeting ..." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will read it out to you. It says: "At the end of the meeting Odja informed that the houses which are most damaged in the areas of Skamala [phoen] in the village of Ljuboten are the ones from which the security forces of the Republic of Macedonia were fired upon by the residents of the aforementioned quarter and that, according to him, this is the reason why the majority of those killed are residents of that quarter; that is, the houses of Veseli Afandi, Jashari Haziz, and Bajrami Qani, and the Zendeli family are located there." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say: "On the other hand, there was also the case of Kamberi, Asad, who set his own house on fire so that he could present himself as a victim of the reaction of the security bodies of the Republic of Macedonia before the international representative." Sir, is Kamberi, Asad, the person which you identified a few minutes ago on the map?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then I will draw your attention to the first comment on the next heading which says: "Contact with Odja was made for the purpose of gaining information in connection with the last year's event around the village of Ljuboten." Sir, did any of the villagers tell you that the reason why a few pockets of the village were targeted was because fire had come from these houses?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So they never mentioned that to you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would simply ask the document be marked for identification at this stage. We'll come back to it in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D87 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, you will recall that you told the Prosecution that you were given information to the effect that two houses, a Macedonian house, that of Mr. Zlatko, and an Albanian house, that of Mr. Kamberi, had been burned on the 16th and 17th of August of 2001; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you will recall also that this information was given to you by some of the villagers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that also correct that you had no independent means to verify whether, in fact, two houses, three houses, or four houses in that street had been burnt on the 16th or 17th of August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown what is 1D32. And simply to clarify, sir, your "yes" was a confirmation to the effect that you were not able to independently verify; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is Exhibit 1D32 with an ERN number N001-5427.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: What is about to appear, Mr. Bouckaert, is a report, an OSCE report of the 17th of August of 2001. Are you able to read it, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a little bit small.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the document -- yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If I may just go through this document with you, it concerns a document of the 17th of August, 2001. It comes from the Operation Office in Skopje to location in Radisani, that was the area covered by the team which covered the village of Ljuboten, and you can see the dates, it says: "Period covered 16 hours, 16 August to 22 hours, 17 August of 2001." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then if you go on to the subheading with the title "Incidents," I'll just read the beginning of that paragraph. It says that: "At approximately 1730, the team arrived in the village of Ljuboten to investigate reports of house fires in the area. Investigation established that at approximately midnight on the 16th and 17th of August, a Macedonian house on the road leading northwest from the church and some 150 metres from the church had burnt." That would be consistent with your evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be the home I identified as Zlatko's home.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: "It was also established that at approximately 11.00 on the 17th August, three Albanian properties had also burnt, one outbuilding and two adjoining houses, all three on the same road as the Macedonian house. How the Macedonian house has been destroyed was unclear. There were no signs of projectile impacts on the wall and no sign of accelerant was observed. A trace of diesel was followed back from the site of the most westerly-destroyed Albanian properties, the two adjoining houses." Sir, would you agree that, in effect, what the OSCE found out was that three Albanian houses and one Macedonian house in that stretch of houses had been burned on the 16th and 17th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The I believe it's one outbuilding and two Albanian houses and the Macedonian house, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then if I may draw your attention to the bottom of that document, it says: "Villagers, both Albanian and elderly Macedonian, confirmed the ethnicity of the property owners. Both Albanian and Macedonian villagers stated that, 'Army paramilitaries,'" -- And then there's parenthesis: "`(Both Albanians and Macedonians were clear that the person referred to were not police) had been in that area of village at the time the Albanian property burned.'" Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Then if I may ask the Registry to bring up what is now P334, Mr. Bouckaert. That's again your own drawing, your own map of the village. First, perhaps to ask you this question, Mr. Bouckaert: The people to whom you talked only mentioned two houses having been burnt on the 16th and 17th; that's your evidence, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: They never mentioned those other two houses having been burnt on this day?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it's possible that the house that they said was burned on Friday contained the outbuilding, but they certainly didn't mention two homes to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And it's also possible that other houses on that stretch of road were burned on the 16th and 17th, you just don't know; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the other homes that are marked on this map, they were burned on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that's based on what you were told by the villagers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And again you had no independent means to verify their information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We based our conclusion on a lot of interviews, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And solely on interviews?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: And on the fact that when we did reach houses that had been burned on different days, it was the villagers who volunteered that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But they didn't volunteer the fact that there were more than two houses that had been burned on the 16th and 17th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They pointed out those houses that are marked on the map to me, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if we may look at your map, if you go to the extreme left bottom side, you will see what you've marked as, I understand, the orthodox church. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it's actually a little bit further down the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's in that general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then if you go northwest of that, you see the house of Zlatko, the one that you had identified as the house of the Macedonian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the houses to which the OSCE refers in its report would appear to be those that would be under the -- what you've marked as "Ulica 5"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where -- it was suggested that the OSCE said that those were burned on other days?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the information I have, and I don't see any indication in the OSCE statement that they're referring to those homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm going to read to you again the passage in question. It says that: "At approximately 7.30 the team arrived in the village of Ljuboten to investigate reports of house fires in the area. Investigation established that at approximately midnight --"

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could we have the document that counsel is reading displayed on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes. If the Registry could bring up what is 1D32, exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, the interpreters are again asking for pauses instead of overlapping of questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, we are warned again. I'll read out this sentence to you again, Mr. Bouckaert. It says: "At approximately 7.30, the team arrived in the village of Ljuboten to investigate reports of house fires in the area. Investigation established that at approximately midnight on 16 and 17 August, a Macedonian house on the road leading northwest from the church and some 150 metres from the church had burnt. It was also established that at approximately 11.00 on the 17th August, three Albanian properties had also burned, one outbuilding and two adjoining houses, all three on the same road as the Macedonian house." So would you agree, sir, that at least so far as the OSCE is concerned, the information which they received was that those three buildings had been burnt in Ulica Pet number 5; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't dispute, be it, that according to the OSCE, the buildings were in Ulica 5. It's not clear for me from their description that they're referring to the buildings in a row which I marked on my map.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So it could have been any three buildings in that street?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you now a few questions about the process of statement-taking which you have explained to the Prosecution and also in your statement to the Prosecution. I have a few questions about that. Is that correct that none of the interviews which you carried out with the victims and witnesses was either audio or videotaped; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that also correct that the procedure that you follow is not technically to take formal statements which are then signed by the victim or the witness, but to take notes into a notebook of yours?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And it's also correct that your notebooks are not signed or otherwise adopted by the people you interview?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And it's also the fact that the report that you then wrote upon your return or during your investigation is based not on any statement but, again, on your note?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: On our interview notes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes. And I think you've indicated to the Prosecution that you speak neither Albanian nor Macedonian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And your interviews with the villagers, your questions to the villagers as well as the response which you received from the villagers, was translated back and forth to through a third party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through my interpreter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that also correct that you were unable to assess for yourself the accuracy of the translation which was given to you by your interpreter at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct to the extent of the period of time after my colleague, Fred Abrahams, left because my colleague Fred Abrahams does speak fluent Albanian and limited Serbian, and he worked together with the same translator, and we never had any indication that there was any problem with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But Fred Abrahams wasn't in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And to answer my question, you were not able to assert for yourself or assess for yourself the accuracy or the quality of the translation which was given to you by the interpreter at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I had no doubt in his objectivity and in his -- the quality of his interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But, again, you were not able to make that assessment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had worked with him for several months, and I had never had a problem with him, so I was quite certain he was doing his job accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But is that correct perhaps that if the interpreter would have made a mistake, you would not have been able to point that out to him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained to Mr. Saxon, we did go over the interviews in the evenings to see if they had been accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But there again, if you go through your notes with the interpreter, the accuracy would be only to his or her understanding of what he or she understood you to say or what the witness answered and what -- not what you understood the witness to answer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I also understand also that you were regularly registered with the Ministry of Information [realtime transcript read in error "Ministry of Internal Affairs"]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you were not what is known in Macedonia as an authorised official; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. There's a mistake in the transcript. It should say "The Ministry of Information" not the "Ministry of Internal Affairs."

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful. And it's at page 40 line 17 and 18. It's the Ministry of Information.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no provision for Human Rights Watch to be registered as an official, so we kind of fell between the cracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But is that correct that you were not accompanied at the time by any authorised official of the State of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's definitely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And none of the statements which you took from -- or none of the notes, in any case, none of the interviews which you made of the villagers was done under oath; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you knew also at the time that the absence of an authorised official would have made those statements inadmissible in local courts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I am not aware of the law in Macedonia on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. But you understood that the persons whom you interviewed were not subject to any form of sanction or perjury for lying to you or otherwise being less than candid with you; is that correct? You understood that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, which is why we conducted many additional interviews to assure the accuracy of our information. Our methodology has been developed to address those kind of concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you would do that through -- I'm going to come back to that, but through the necessary requirement for you to corroborate each and every incident for which you were given evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you draw to the attention of the villagers whom you interviewed the fact that those statements that they made to you could be used in the context of criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did draw -- as is our general practice, I informed the people that we interviewed that I was investigating what happened in Ljuboten and that their statements could be used in our report, and I also asked them if it was okay to use their names in our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And did you also point that to them that these statements could be used in the context of criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can I ask you whether you have been or whether you have been asked by the Prosecution could give copies of those notes of yours which you took in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked. It's the general practice of our organisation, and I'm under instructions from our organisation, that we don't hand over our notes, which is why our statement was submitted under Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But isn't it correct that in Human Rights Watch, there is in fact a procedure in place for a party to request these notes from you; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I'll simply read a statement from your colleague's -- Fred Abrahams', from the Milatinovic proceedings, and perhaps I will call it so that you can see for yourself. It's under 1D003812. It's from the transcript of 13th of July, 2006, and it's at page 904. This is what Mr. Abrahams said to the Trial Chamber in the Milatinovic case. I'll wait until the document is in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's the ERN number is 1D003812.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, in the absence of the document, I'll show it to you later on, but for the time being I'll simply read the statement of Mr. Abrahams, and we can look at it after the break. Mr. Abrahams is recorded as saying this: "As a matter of policy, the notes are the private property of the organisation," and that's Human Rights Watch, "but individuals or organisation can make specific requests to our legal office for a release, which will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis." Is that a correct statement of the procedure and the practice before Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the property of the organisation. It's our general practice not to release notes. Any exception to that rule would have to be made by our legal office rather than by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And was such a request made for the notes that you took in the village of Ljuboten by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, an informal request was made, and it was denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And was the formal procedure which I read to you followed as well, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OTP accepted that we had the right to keep our notes confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you a few questions about the procedure and mechanism which are in place at Human Rights Watch to ensure the quality of your reporting. Am I correct that, in a way, Human Rights Watch is a self-regulated body, and by that I mean that there is no outside body which assess the quality or intervenes into the quality of your product?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The quality of our product is certainly publicly assessed by a wide variety of sources, including the public, including the diplomatic community, and we would quickly lose the effectiveness of our organisation if the quality of our information was challenged.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps my question should have been more precise. When you prepare a report, such as the report that we've discussed beforehand, is that correct that the process or the involvement of individuals into the preparation, the drafting, the editing, and so on of the document is limited to employees and staff members of Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be generally correct, although on many occasions we do use outside experts to evaluate reports, especially technical reports about illegal arms trades and other such issues. But we have an extensive in-house review process of our reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And did you have recourse to any outside help or assistance in relation to the Ljuboten report?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in relation to the Ljuboten report.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Am I correct to understand that one of the most fundamental safeguards, so to say, of the quality of your reports is your insistence to rely on primary evidence rather than hearsay or secondary evidence?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And another safeguard is for you to have recourse to as many and as rich a variety of sources as possible?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you've also just indicated that there is an internal vetting procedure which you have described in your statement as being quite stringent to ensure that the material contained in every report is supported by the material which you've collected during your investigation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The report is first reviewed by the regional division or the Tomatic [phoen] Division, which has oversight over the work, in this case that would have been the Europe and Central Asia Division, it was refused by the Executive Director of the Europe and Central Asia Division, then it is reviewed by the Legal Division of Human Rights Watch, by legal counsel with extensive experience in human rights law and the laws of war, and then it is reviewed by our Programme Division which oversees all of the work of the organisation. And in some exceptional cases, it's also reviewed by the Executive Director.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that correct that if at any stage in that process any of the layers of control, so to say, is not satisfied about the sufficiency or the reliability of any of that material, the material would then be withheld from the public; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. They would ask me to go back and do further research, perhaps, on a certain point, or if it was the case of a legal conclusion, we would abide by the decision of our legal office. But certainly your point is correct that we would not include unreliable information in our reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in the case of the Ljuboten reports, were you asked by any of -- anyone in your hierarchy to do any further research or investigation when after you had given them your draft report?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have to go do any further interviews. I wasn't asked to do any additional interviews, but certainly there were many questions asked, many requests for clarification, and many discussions before the report was finalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And we've just discussed it, but I would like to spend a bit more time on it. One of the fundamental safeguards, so to say, of your procedure is the requirement that every fact which you state in your report or every incident that you report about is being corroborated at least by two sources, I understand, or one source plus corroboration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's overstating things a little bit. In our report, there certainly are incidents which are based on the evidence of a single witness, but then the text of the report would indicate that we had no further witnesses available and that some questions remain to be answered. And in those cases, the statement of that single witness will be corroborated with physical evidence or other evidence available to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So am I correct to understand from your answer that the availability or otherwise of corroborating evidence would be obvious from the mere reading of the footnote in your report?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that our report reflects the nature of the evidence that we have available to us, either in the text or in the footnote, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So if a fact is stated in your report or a finding is being made by you in a report, the source of that finding and the entirety of the source of that finding would be traceable either in the text or in the footnote of the finding; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that was the case with your report on Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless sources ask for anonymity.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Which was the case on a number of occasions, two or three occasions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and in that case we would keep their names on record at Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that also correct that the need for corroboration of evidence and the care which you pay to that matter is particularly important when you interview members of a particular group or community which report violations or violence against other members of that same community; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that also correct that you were aware, particularly because of your experience in Kosovo, that members of the Albanian community could be subject to particular pressure from the NLA, the UCK, not to reveal or to give a particular versions of the events; that's something you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did very extensive work in Kosovo, but before, during, and after the NATO bombing of Kosovo, and as far as I know all of our reports remain accurate to date, have never been seriously challenged, so obviously our methodology has been designed to deal with those -- the kind of challenges you describe.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But perhaps to answer my question, you were aware of the fact that UCK or the NLA, or the KLA in the case of Kosovo, was at the time exercising great pressure on the citizens of the Albanian members of the population to give a particular account of the events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't just limit it to the UCK. There were such cases on all sides of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But that would be the case with the UCK; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure there were such cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Mettraux?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must have the first break and resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, I have been threatened with all sorts of unpleasant consequences during the break by the poor interpreter, who have been put under great strain, so if we can attempt to not overlap, and I would be grateful if you would assist me in that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I mention, Mr. Mettraux, it's not merely, I suspect, the matter of overlap, but when you come to read a long passage, you have quite a quick delivery.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That may be correct, Your Honour. I'll ask the Registry, just in fairness to Mr. Bouckaert, that he be shown what is or what has been identified as Rule 65 ter 424. It has an ERN of 1D003812.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
